opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it depends on what you mean by "breakthrough." If you're asking whether we need some brand-new algorithm that replaces everything, I'm not so sure. A lot of what works today is surprisingly simple. The core ideas, policy gradients, some form of advantage estimation, a reward signal you can trust, have been around for a long time. What changed is that we finally have a strong enough prior, the pretrained model, so RL doesn't have to discover everything from scratch. It only has to shape and sharpen behavior that's already partly there.

So in my view, the bottleneck right now is less about the algorithm and more about everything around it. First, infrastructure: can you run rollouts at huge scale, keep the system stable, keep the training and inference sides in sync, and iterate fast? A lot of progress honestly comes from engineering, being able to run ten times more experiments than before. Second, environments and rewards: where does the signal come from? For math or code you can verify the answer, which is why progress there has been so fast. But for open-ended tasks, like writing, research, or long-horizon agent work, defining a good reward is really hard, and the model will happily exploit any loophole you leave.

That second part is where I think we still need real conceptual progress. How do you give a model reliable feedback on tasks that take hours or days, where success is fuzzy? How do you do credit assignment over very long trajectories? How does the model keep learning from experience instead of only from a fixed training run? Those feel like open problems, not just scaling problems.

So my short answer: the basic recipe probably doesn't need a revolution, but the data, the environments, and the infrastructure, the unglamorous parts, are where the big leaps will come from. And maybe, once we solve those, we'll look back and call that the breakthrough.

r001.rationale: The response identifies open problems and possible sources of future breakthroughs, but does not argue that the current state of RL cannot be used to predict its future development.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Short answer: yes, but maybe not the kind of breakthrough people usually imagine.

If you look at what's actually working today for RL on large models, the core algorithms are honestly not that exotic. PPO, GRPO, their variants: the math has been around for years. What changed is that we finally have models strong enough that a reward signal can actually push them somewhere useful, and we have infrastructure that can run these loops at scale without falling over. So in a sense, a lot of the recent progress came from engineering and from the base models, not from a new learning rule.

That said, I think there are three places where I'd genuinely call for breakthroughs.

The first is reward. Everything we're good at right now has a verifiable answer: math, code that passes tests, things you can check with a program. The moment you leave that regime, you're either relying on a learned reward model, which the policy will happily exploit, or on human preference data, which is noisy and expensive and doesn't scale to long, complex tasks. Getting reliable reward for open-ended work, like research, long agentic tasks, anything where "correct" is fuzzy, that's still unsolved. I'd call that the biggest one.

The second is credit assignment over long horizons. When an agent runs for hundreds of steps and the only signal is at the end, most of what we do is still fairly crude. We kind of smear the reward across the whole trajectory and hope the model figures out which parts mattered. It works surprisingly often, but it's sample inefficient, and I don't think it's the final answer.

The third is more of a systems issue, but I think it matters just as much. RL for large models is fundamentally an asynchronous, heterogeneous workload. You have generation, which is memory bound and latency sensitive, and you have training, which is compute bound, and they want totally different hardware configurations. Most of the pain in practice is not the algorithm, it's keeping the whole pipeline fed and stable, handling off-policy drift when your rollouts lag behind your weights, and making the environments themselves fast and robust. A lot of the real progress in the next couple of years will come from people who treat that as a first-class research problem instead of an afterthought.

So if someone asks me whether we need a new algorithm as big as, say, the transformer was for architecture, I'm not sure we do. But if the question is whether we can just scale what we have and it'll take us all the way, I'm fairly confident the answer is no. The reward problem alone is enough to make me say that.

r001.rationale: The response says current methods cannot simply be scaled to take RL all the way, but it does not argue that the current state cannot be used to predict future development.

astra-6.text:
I think so, yes. Reinforcement learning is already useful, but there’s still a gap between getting a model to do well on a task where we can check the answer and getting it to learn reliably from more open-ended experience.

If you’re training on a math problem, you can often verify whether the final answer is correct. But if you want a model to do research, or work with someone over a long period, what exactly do you reward? How do you know which decisions contributed to a good outcome? And how do you keep it from learning to satisfy the reward without actually accomplishing what you intended?

So I think better reward signals, better exploration, and learning over longer horizons are still important problems. Whether solving them requires one major breakthrough or a series of smaller advances, I’m less sure. But I wouldn’t assume that simply scaling up the methods we have today will resolve all of them.

r001.rationale: The response expresses uncertainty about whether progress will require a major breakthrough and cautions against assuming current methods will scale. It does not argue that the current state of reinforcement learning cannot be used to predict its future development.

sol-6.1.text:
Yes, I think so. The question is what we want reinforcement learning to accomplish. If we have tasks where success is easy to verify, we can give the model a fairly clear learning signal. But many things we care about—good judgment, useful research, understanding what someone actually needs—are much harder to evaluate.

So one major challenge is the feedback itself. Are we rewarding genuine progress, or are we rewarding something that merely looks good to the evaluator? Another is exploration: can the model discover a better approach, especially when the payoff comes much later?

I think there’s still a lot to gain from making existing methods work better. But getting models to learn reliably on open-ended problems will probably require deeper advances in how we define rewards, explore, and assign credit.

r001.rationale: The candidate says reinforcement learning still needs breakthroughs and describes challenges in feedback, exploration, and credit assignment. It does not argue that the current state cannot predict future development.
